phonemes.desc: Voiceless bilabial stop [p] released directly into a trilled [r] — a clean initial cluster with no vowel between, as in English 'prince'.
The Welsh obscure vowel [ə], the 'clear y' of non-final syllables — a soft central 'uh', never the [i] of the final position.
Voiced [d] and open-mid [ɛ] with a tapped [r], carrying the stress: Welsh words are stressed on the penultimate syllable, so the weight of the name lands here.
Short close [i], the unstressed final vowel, closing quietly.

pronunciation.approximation: 'pruh-DEH-ree' — the y is a soft 'uh', the stress falls on 'der' (the Welsh penult), and the final i is a short 'ee'.

kin.label: Middle Welsh
kin.form: Pryderi uab Pwyll, son of Pwyll Pen Annwn and Rhiannon, lord of Dyfed in the Four Branches of the Mabinogi.

kin.label: Foster-name
kin.form: Gwri Wallt Euryn, 'Gwri of the Golden Hair' — the name Teyrnon Twrf Liant's household gave the foundling before his true name was known.

kin.label: Welsh common noun
kin.form: pryder, 'care, anxiety, worry' — the living word the First Branch names him from: Rhiannon's own pryder, lifted at his return.

kin.label: Comparative reflex
kin.form: Mabon ap Modron, the Welsh divine son stolen from his mother, and Gaulish Maponos — the figure-type Pryderi is read against; a parallel, not a cognate of the name.

pronunciation.note: Pryderi is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the Middle Welsh form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, and only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input. The name's etymology is the tale's own: the First Branch names him from Rhiannon's word pryder, 'care, anxiety', spoken when the lost child was restored — an aetiological naming the medieval author builds into the story itself, and the lexicon's gloss 'Care, anxiety' follows the text.

domains.title: The Lord Who Spans the Four Branches
domains.subtitle: Son of Pwyll, King
domains.lead: Pryderi is the hinge of the whole Mabinogi: the only figure who walks through all Four Branches — stolen on the night of his birth and found outside a stable door, named from his mother's lifted anxiety, emptied out of Dyfed by an enchanter's mist, and killed at last in single combat by Gwydion's craft. Son of Pwyll and Rhiannon, lord of Dyfed, he is the king the tales keep taking things from — and the name he carries is the Welsh word for care.

cards.name: The Stable Door
cards.desc: Outside Teyrnon's stable, where a great clawed hand had come for the newborn foal, lay an infant wrapped in silk brocade — the stolen heir of Dyfed.

cards.name: The Naming
cards.desc: Rhiannon looks at the boy and says her pryder — her care, her anxiety — is lifted from her; from that word the child is named Pryderi.

cards.name: The Golden Bowl
cards.desc: Hanging by chains above a marble fountain in a fortress that was never there before: when Pryderi grasps it, his hands stick, his feet root to the slab, and his voice dies.

cards.name: The First Swine
cards.desc: The hobeu, first pigs ever brought to Wales — Arawn of Annwn's gift to the house of Pwyll — which Gwydion wins with illusory gold and pays for with Pryderi's life.

symbols.name: The silk brocade wrapping
symbols.meaning: Royal blood declaring itself at a stable door — the foundling child whose swaddling says what no witness can

symbols.name: The clawed hand
symbols.meaning: The Otherworld reaching through the window on May-eve — the unseen power that takes foals and princes alike

symbols.name: The golden bowl on its chains
symbols.meaning: Bait that looks like treasure — the trap at the heart of the enchanted fortress, and the cost of touching what is not yours

symbols.name: The gate-hammer about his neck
symbols.meaning: What he wore out of the enchantment — the humiliation of the Third Branch, borne home and buried in silence

symbols.name: The swine of Annwn
symbols.meaning: Otherworld wealth with a geis upon it — not to be sold or given until the herd had doubled — and the war a broken promise bought

symbols.name: The grave at Maen Tywynog
symbols.meaning: The mound above Y Felenrhyd where the slain lord was buried — the one fixed point of a life lived under enchantment

mythology.lead: Pryderi's mythology is unique in Welsh prose: he is the only character who appears in all Four Branches of the Mabinogi, and his life is the thread the whole cycle is strung on. The First Branch gives his birth, theft, and naming; the Second carries him through the Irish war as one of the seven survivors; the Third empties his kingdom and takes him captive; the Fourth kills him. Every word of it is medieval Welsh prose, preserved in two great manuscripts.

myths.title: The May-Eve Vanishing
myths.text: Pryderi is born to Pwyll and Rhiannon after the nobles of Dyfed have pressed for an heir, and on the night of his birth the six women set to watch all fall asleep — and the child is gone. Terrified of the blame, the women kill the pups of a hound, smear the blood on Rhiannon's face, lay the bones beside her, and swear she has destroyed her own son; her penance at the horse-block begins, and it will last until the boy comes home. The child, meanwhile, has fallen into the strangest rescue in Welsh prose. Teyrnon Twrf Liant, a lord of Gwent Is Coed by the sea, loses a foal every May-eve; keeping watch over his mare, he sees a great clawed hand reach through the window to seize the newborn foal, and strikes it off with his sword. Outside the door he finds a baby boy wrapped in silk brocade. He and his wife rear the child as their own and call him Gwri Wallt Euryn — Gwri of the Golden Hair.

myths.title: The Naming at Arberth
myths.text: Gwri grows with uncanny speed — at the end of his first year sturdier than a child of three, at two like a boy of six — and year by year he bears the very likeness of Pwyll. When Teyrnon hears of Rhiannon's penance, he knows what he must do, and he and his wife bring the boy to Arberth. The court sees the likeness at once, and Rhiannon says that if this is true, her pryder — her care, her anxiety — is lifted from her. Pwyll declares that the boy should take his name from the word his mother spoke when the news was brought to her, and so the child is named Pryderi. The penance ends; Teyrnon will take no reward beyond the boy's friendship; and Pryderi is fostered with Pendaran Dyfed until he is of age, when Pwyll gives him the realm.

myths.title: One of the Seven
myths.text: When Bendigeidfran — Brân the Blessed — leads the host of Britain into Ireland to answer the wrong done to Branwen, the war ends in near-total ruin: the Irish are destroyed, and of the host of the Island of the Mighty only seven men come back alive, bearing Brân's wounded head. The tale names them, and the first two it names are Pryderi and Manawydan, with Glifieu, Taliesin, Ynawg, Gruddieu, and Heilyn. With the others Pryderi feasts seven years at Harlech, where the Birds of Rhiannon sing, and eighty years at Gwales in Penfro in the Assembly of the Wondrous Head — a man who has sailed out of his own branch into the middle of someone else's tragedy, and who carries its grief home into the Third.

myths.title: The Enchantment of Dyfed
myths.text:
After Pwyll's death, Pryderi rules Dyfed and gives his mother Rhiannon in marriage to Manawydan fab Llŷr; with his wife Cigfa, the four come home to Arberth. There comes a peal of thunder and a fall of mist, and when it lifts, Dyfed is emptied — not a person, not a dwelling, not a beast remains. For two years the four live by hunting; then they try saddlery, shield-making, and shoemaking in the towns of England, and each time the local craftsmen drive them out for making work too good to allow. Back in empty Dyfed, a shining white boar leads Pryderi and Manawydan to a fortress that was never there before. Against Manawydan's counsel Pryderi goes in, lays hold of a golden bowl hanging by chains above a marble fountain — and his hands stick to the bowl, his feet to the slab, and speech leaves him. Rhiannon goes in after him, takes hold of the same bowl, and is caught beside him; fort, bowl, and both prisoners vanish.

Manawydan undoes the spell by patience: sowing wheat, he catches the one slow mouse stripping his third ripe field, condemns it to hang as a thief, and names his price to the bishop who comes to beg it off — Pryderi and Rhiannon released, the enchantment lifted from Dyfed, and no vengeance taken for it. The mouse is the wife of Llwyd fab Cilcoed, who had laid the spell to avenge his friend Gwawl fab Clud, the suitor Rhiannon refused. Pryderi comes home with a gate-hammer about his neck, and Rhiannon with the collars of asses about hers; the land wakes, and the Third Branch ends with the four of them feasting as they began.

myths.title: The Swine and the Fatal Combat
myths.text: Among Pryderi's treasures are the hobeu, the first swine ever brought to Wales — a gift to his house from Arawn of Annwn, which Pryderi had sworn neither to sell nor to give until the herd had bred twice its number. Gwydion fab Dôn comes to his court in the guise of a poet, is refused the pigs, and conjures twelve stallions with golden harness, twelve greyhounds with golden collars and leashes, and twelve golden shields — apparitions good for a day and gone by morning — and trades them for the herd. When the glamour fades, Pryderi musters Dyfed and comes north, and the war that follows forces the crime Gwydion and Gilfaethwy commit against Goewin. At the peace-talks Pryderi demands single combat, for it was because of him the hosts had come; at Y Felenrhyd, the tale says, Gwydion slew him 'by strength and valour, and by magic and enchantment'. They buried Pryderi there, at Maen Tywynog above Y Felenrhyd — and his grave, the Fourth Branch says, is there.

lore.syncretism: Pryderi's great comparative frame is the Celtic divine son. The handbooks set him beside Mabon ap Modron — 'Son son of Mother' — the youth of Culhwch ac Olwen who was taken from his mother Modron when he was three nights old and found again after a search that outlasts every living memory, and behind Mabon the Gaulish Maponos, the 'Divine Son' whom Romano-Celtic dedications pair with Apollo. A child of an Otherworld mother, stolen at birth and restored, whose name carries his story: the figure-type is one, and Mac Cana and Koch both register the comparison — but the names are not cognate, and no scholar claims identity. The second frame is sovereignty-by-loss: like the stricken kings of Irish tradition, Pryderi holds a kingdom that enchantment can empty in a night, and his rescue comes not by his own strength but by Manawydan's patience — the Third Branch's quiet thesis about where a king's real safety lies. Within the corpus his closest kin are his parents [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]] and Pwyll Pen Annwn, his stepfather and rescuer [[manawydan|Manawydan]], his benefactor [[arawn|Arawn]] of [[annwn|Annwn]], and his slayer [[gwydion|Gwydion]] — the enchanter whose conjured wealth bought the pigs and, with them, the war.
lore.culturalLegacy: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried Pryderi out of the Welsh manuscripts and into English, and the Victorian Celtic revival made the vanished child of the First Branch one of its set-pieces. Twentieth-century scholarship gave him his modern standing: Ifor Williams's edition fixed the standard Welsh text, W. J. Gruffydd's Rhiannon (1953) built its whole argument about the First and Third Branches around the Pryderi complex, and Mac Cana's study of the Mabinogi made the boy who spans all four branches the structural key to the cycle. Evangeline Walton's Mabinogion tetralogy retold his theft and naming for modern readers, and Lloyd Alexander's Chronicles of Prydain — five novels built openly on the Mabinogi's world — carried the matter of Pryderi's branches to a vast young readership, though the boy himself never appears under his own name. In modern Druid and pagan practice he is honoured as the lost-and-found divine son and the lord who endured the emptied land, and the name survives in scholarship as the standing example of the Mabinogi's own method: a person named, deliberately and explicitly, out of a single spoken word of grief relieved.
lore.extendedMeditation: Pryderi is named out of relief. His mother has carried a false charge for years — sitting by the horse-block, offering her back to strangers — and when the lost boy is set before her she does not say vengeance, or justice, or even joy: she says her care is lifted, and the court builds the child's name out of that word. Anxiety, made into a name and then, astonishingly, into a king. The rest of his story keeps faith with the naming. His is the kingdom a mist can empty between one hour and the next; his is the hand that sticks to the golden bowl; his is the herd of otherworld pigs that a poet's illusion can buy; his is the grave above Y Felenrhyd. Nothing in the Four Branches is safe, and Pryderi is the figure through whom the Mabinogi says so — the lord who loses everything except the thread of the tale, and who walks through all four branches carrying it. Care, the Welsh word means; and also what care is for: the watch kept, the debt counted, the mother who waited at the gate.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Pryderi — attested in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410), the two great manuscripts of the Mabinogi. Middle Welsh writes the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, which is why the name stands in Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: pryderi.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none. The temple is served at /sites/pryderi/ in the meantime.

lore.archaeology: Pryderi is a textual figure: no temple, votive deposit, or inscription names him, and the early inscribed stones of Wales — Latin and ogham memorial stones of roughly the fifth to seventh centuries — record personal names in funerary formulae, not the heroes of story. His evidence is manuscript evidence. The Four Branches survive complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410), with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6; the tales' date of composition is argued rather than documented — Ifor Williams placed them in the later eleventh century, and current scholarship generally holds a range around 1060–1120. The geography of his story is real and walkable: Arberth, the chief court of Dyfed, stands by modern Narberth in Pembrokeshire; Y Felenrhyd, where the fatal combat was fought, lies in the country toward the border of Gwynedd and Dyfed; and the Fourth Branch points to his grave at Maen Tywynog above it. The nearest epigraphic horizon is comparative, not his: the Gaulish Maponos of the Chamalières tablet and the northern British dedications to Apollo Maponus — the divine son whose figure-type the handbooks read him against.
